topic: Simon Baron-Cohen, Alan Leslie & Uta Frith (1985): The 'Sally-Anne' Marble Transfer & Theory of Mind
visual_mode_reason: Moving a shiny glass marble from Sally's wicker basket into Anne's cardboard box across a tabletop puppet stage is instantly visual, paired with temporoparietal / medial-prefrontal mentalizing development.

primary_case.title: Baron-Cohen, Leslie & Frith's 1985 'Sally-Anne' false-belief puppet experiment

people.name: Simon Baron-Cohen
people.role: Developmental psychopathologist who co-created the Sally-Anne puppet adaptation of Wimmer & Perner's false-belief task

people.name: Alan M. Leslie & Uta Frith
people.role: MRC London cognitive scientists who co-theorized metarepresentation and decoupled mental-state tracking

people.name: Heinz Wimmer & Josef Perner
people.role: Developmental psychologists who invented the original 1983 Maxi-and-the-chocolate false-belief paradigm

core_facts.fact: Building on Premack & Woodruff (1978) and Wimmer & Perner's 1983 chocolate story, Simon Baron-Cohen, Alan Leslie, and Uta Frith created the minimalist 'Sally-Anne' tabletop doll test at London's MRC Cognitive Development Unit in 1985.
The child sits across from two small dolls: Sally (who has a round covered basket) and Anne (who has a rectangular covered box).
Sally places a glass marble inside her basket and walks out of the room; while Sally is GONE, mischievous Anne lifts the marble out of the basket and hides it inside Anne's own closed box.

Before asking the test question, researchers verify two control questions ('Where is the marble REALLY right now?' — Box; 'Where was the marble in the beginning?' — Basket) — passed 100 percent by every group.
Then Sally returns, and the researcher asks the decisive Belief Question: 'Where will Sally LOOK for her marble?'
Passing requires holding TWO contradictory realities in your head at once: YOU know the marble is in the box, yet SALLY falsely believes it is still in her basket because she didn't see the swap.

Across typical developmental studies (Wellman et al. 2001 meta-analysis of 178 studies), 3-year-olds reliably fail verbal false-belief questions (~80% point to the box where the marble really is!), whereas by age 4.5 roughly 85 percent pass effortlessly (23 of 27 typical 4-year-olds and 12 of 14 children with Down syndrome of lower verbal mental age passed in 1985, while 16 of 20 autistic children in that high-support 1985 clinical sample pointed to the box).

Crucial modern update (Gernsbacher & Yergeau 2019; Milton's Double Empathy Problem; Baron-Cohen 2025): eye-tracking and modern replications proved 1) many autistic youths and adults pass verbal false-belief tasks cleanly depending on language load; 2) non-autistic people struggle JUST as hard to read autistic expressions ('two-way Double Empathy mismatch', not one-way brokenness); and 3) EVERY healthy adult routinely slips into the exact same 'Curse of Knowledge' error when writing confusing emails.

wow_facts.fact: Ask a bright three-year-old 'Where will Sally look for her marble?' right after Anne secretly moved it, and the three-year-old points straight to the new box — completely unable to imagine Sally doesn't know what THEY just saw.
wow_facts.why_surprising: Separating 'what is true' from 'what someone else believes' is a developmental leap between ages 3 and 5.

wow_facts.fact: Every child in the room answered 'Where is the marble REALLY?' and 'Where did it start?' at 100 percent accuracy — the ONLY hurdle was decoupling someone else's unseen mental model from reality.
wow_facts.why_surprising: Memory and eyesight were spotless; perspective decoupling was the puzzle.

wow_facts.fact: Modern researchers (Damian Milton; Gernsbacher) overturned 1990s 'universal mindblindness' overgeneralizations by testing the reverse direction: neurotypical observers misread autistic people's emotions and intentions at high rates too ('the Double Empathy Problem').
wow_facts.why_surprising: Misunderstanding across different minds runs on a two-way street.

wow_facts.fact: Even PhD adults fail adult versions of Sally-Anne every single day — tapping out 'Happy Birthday' on a table and guessing listeners hear the tune 50 percent of the time when actual listeners guess just 2.5 percent ('Curse of Knowledge').
wow_facts.why_surprising: Once you know where the marble is, forgetting you know it takes effort at any age.

misconceptions.myth: Three-year-olds point to Anne's box because they forgot where Sally put the marble.
misconceptions.truth: They pass the 'Where was it at the beginning?' memory check 100% of the time; reality-bias overrides false-belief decoupling.

misconceptions.myth: Every autistic person lacks empathy or fails Theory of Mind tasks.
misconceptions.truth: That outdated stereotype collapsed under empirical scrutiny (SRC1): affective care/empathy is distinct from rapid social cueing, language demands heavily skew Sally-Anne scores, and misunderstanding between neurotypes is bidirectional ('Double Empathy').

misconceptions.myth: Once you turn five, you never confuse your own knowledge with someone else's again.
misconceptions.truth: Adults constantly fall for the 'Curse of Knowledge' — writing cryptic acronyms or directions assuming readers see the map inside the writer's head.

misconceptions.myth: Theory of Mind is a single binary switch you either have or don't.
misconceptions.truth: Mentalizing spans graded skills from eye-gaze tracking to second-order beliefs ('Alice thinks Bob thinks...') and taxing tired adult prefrontal resources.

everyday_hooks: Sending a three-word Slack message ('Check the doc!') assuming your teammate knows which of forty docs you just had open ('adult Sally-Anne error').
Watching a 3-year-old play hide-and-seek by covering ONLY their own eyes in the middle of the rug ('if I can't see you, you can't see me').
Practicing 'Double Empathy' humility: asking directly what a colleague meant instead of assuming everyone signals feelings with identical body language.
Reading a draft email pretending you do NOT know the secret move Anne made in Paragraph 3.
